The Michigan State Police Recently Took Police Cars To A Track To See Which Was Fastest

TB
By Tyler Brooks Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead • via Jalopnik Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Jalopnik Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset
⚡ Executive Takeaways & Key Highlights

  • Yet as the Michigan State Police found out this fall, those motors can still be impressively effective.

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • TYLER BROOKS Viral Concepts & Prototype Lead

Automotive Innovation & Market Feasibility

Concept prototypes and viral vehicle reveals offer an exciting window into the automotive industry's future design language. Dispatches from Jalopnik demonstrate how radical styling, lightweight materials, and powertrain packaging can transition from design studios to production assembly lines. Engineering feasibility and homologation standards remain the true measures of impact.

Big Picture: Market reception and formal OEM production announcements will determine which concept innovations make it to consumer streets.

We've looked at five features that make police cars different from their civilian counterparts, and concluded they don't really get better engines . Yet as the Michigan State Police found out this fall, those motors can still be impressively effective. Their testing was part of an annual program that dates back to 1975 and over the years has become an industry benchmark.

📌 The Core Development

This time around, 13 cars — and five motorcycles — were put through their paces on two separate courses. Chelsea Proving Ground, located in Chelsea, MI., and owned by Stellantis, was used to evaluate the vehicles' top speed, acceleration, and braking. Vehicle dynamics were tested at Grattan Raceway in Belding, MI. Incidentally, the historic Grattan track was for sale when this article was written, with a listing price of a cool $15 million.

As for the fastest, that was the all-wheel-drive Ford Police Interceptor Utility. It leveraged its 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6 — making 400 horsepower and 415 pound-feet of torque – to hit an electronically limited 148 mph. That was faster than the faster police motorcycle, too. On the two-wheeled side of the ledger, the leader was the BMW R 1300 RT-P in its standard setup — with a maximum velocity of 141 mph that was again electronically limited. In fact, all the vehicles in the test had top speeds limited by manufacturers.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The results are nothing new, though. The Blue Oval's Interceptor Utility has been the fastest car in the Michigan State Police ranks since it shared that honor with the Dodge Charger back in 2020. Rounding out the 2026 top 6 for top speed were the AWD Ford Police Interceptor with hybrid and gas-only powertrains, both listed at 136 mph, and the RWD Chevrolet Tahoe PPV with the 5.3-liter V8, the Chevrolet Blazer PPV EV with AWD, and the Dodge Durango Pursuit with a 5.7-liter V8 and AWD. That trio clocked in at 130 mph.

Of course, top speed is only one important criteria for police performance, so the MSP went on to measure the vehicles' 0 – 60 sprint times — even though tracking a car going from 5 – 60 is usually a superior performance metric . Anyways, results here went about the way you might have expected once you realized not one but two EVs were on the test roster. The nearly instant torque delivered by the Blazer EV and the AWD Ford Mustang Mach-E GT helped them set the bar for acceleration: The former measured at 5.14 seconds and the latter leading the way at a brisk 4.03 seconds.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

Ford's PIU with the 3.0-liter EcoBoost and the Ford F-150 Police Responder, which upsizes to a 3.5-liter EcoBoost mill, are the only other non-motorcycles to get in under 6 seconds. The quickest police cars with internal combustion engines did the job in 5.95 and 5.68 seconds, respectively. The quickest motorcycle, the BMW 1300 R-PT with the Dynamic Pack and AutoShift, was then the only vehicle to break the 4.0-second mark. It finished the sprint in only 3.61 seconds.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

It's also worth pointing out that the MSP checked 0-to-100 times, with pretty much the same results. The quickest EV was again the Mach-E, the two quickest gas-powered cars were the Ford PIU and F-150 Police Responder, and the quickest bike was the BMW with the Dynamic Pack/AutoShift.

Considering how dangerous high-speed pursuits are , a good set of stoppers and superior vehicle dynamics are vital for police vehicles as well. With that in mind, the MSP put its test vehicles through multiple "60 – 0 mph full ABS maximum deceleration stops" to come up with a final projected stopping distance from that speed. The Mustang Mach-E came out on top in this testing, bolstered by a projected stopping distance of 122.45 feet. No other vehicle tested was below 130 feet. Moreover, one pass with the Mach-E saw the car go from 59.7 mph to a complete halt in 116.75 feet. Meanwhile, the MSP's fastest police vehicle — the Ford PIU with the 3.0-liter EcoBoost — had the seventh-shortest stopping-distance projection, at 137.24 feet. The 2026 Ram 2500, with four-wheel drive and a 6.4-liter V8, provides some context with a projected stopping distance of 170.13 feet that was by far the longest in the MSP testing.
